﴿then as for whoever transgressed,﴾ ﴿and preferred the worldly life,﴾ ﴿indeed Hellfire will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿But as for whoever feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire,﴾ ﴿indeed Paradise will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained but an evening or a morning.﴾

(p. 417) *Aghraqa fi al-shay'*: he went to the utmost extent in it and reached its end. *Aghraqa al-nazi'* *fi al-qaws*: the archer pulled the bowstring to its full extent until it reached the arrow-head. *Al-istighraq* means comprehensive inclusion, and *al-gharqa* is the shell of an egg. *Nashata al-ba'ir wa al-insan*: he tied the camel or the man. *Anshatahu*: he released him. From this comes the phrase "as if he had been released from a tether." *Nashita*: he went from one region to another. For this reason wild cattle are called *al-nawashit*, because they travel swiftly from place to place. From this is the verse of the poet, who is Himyan ibn Qahafa:

*I see my worries driving the places before me; at times they carry me to Syria, at times to Wasit.*

It seems this word is derived from *al-nashat* (activity). Abu Zayd said: *nashastu al-habl anshuṭuhu nashṭan*: I tied it into a slipknot (*unshuṭa*). *Anshaṭtu*: I untied it. *Anshaṭtu al-habl*: I stretched it. Al-Layth said: *anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭa*: I fastened it, meaning I secured it. *Anshaṭtu al-'iqal*: I stretched its slipknot so that it came undone. It is said that *nashita* has the same meaning as *anshaṭa*. The *unshuṭa* is a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a waistband.

*Wajafa al-qalb wa jiyafan*: the heart pounded from the intensity of fear. Likewise *wajaba wa jiyaban*. In the book *Lughat al-Qur'an* (The Languages of the Qur'an), attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, *wajifa* means "fearful," in the dialect of Hamdan. *Al-hafira*: it is said, "So-and-so returned along his *hafira*," meaning on the path by which he came, since his footsteps have left marks (*hafr*) on it. The Arabs apply the term to the first state to which one returns from its end. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Would you return to the first state with baldness and grey hair? God forbid such folly and shame!*

That is, "Shall I return to youth after baldness and gray hair?"

*Al-nakhira*: that which produces sound through the wind, hollow. *Al-nakhira* has the same meaning, like *ṭami'* and *ṭamia*, *ḥadhir* and *ḥadhar*. This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and a group. It was also said: *al-nakhira* is what is decayed, rotten, and turned into dust. *Nakhira al-'ud wa al-'aẓm*: it decayed and crumbled, and its meaning differs from *al-nakhira*. This is the view of most scholars. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: *al-nakhira* is what has not yet become hollow, and *al-nakhira* is what has already decayed. A rajaz poet said to his horse:

*Advance, brother of the fierce, toward the trials,*
*and let not the heads of the rebels frighten you.*
*Your end is only the dust of the desert,*
*until you return after that to the pit,*
*after you have become hollow bones.*

Another poet said:

*I emptied it of its marrow, so it became like glass vessels in whose hollows the wind whistles.*

It is also narrated as "whistles" (*tuṣaffiru*). *Nukhrat al-rih* (with a *ḍamma* on the *nun*) means the violence of its blowing. *Al-nukhra* also means the front of the nose of a horse, donkey, or pig. One says: "He broke its nukhra." *Al-sahira*: the surface of the earth and the open wilderness. It is described by what happens in it, which is wakefulness (*al-sahar*) due to fear. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*In it is the flesh of the wilderness and the sea, and what they have said remains for them.*

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said:

*They walk in the wilderness, as though its tresses and its locks were the dark garments of a black night.*

*Al-sahur* is like a sheath for the moon, which enters it when it is eclipsed. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said: (p. 418)

*He spread creation upon it when He spread it out, and they are its inhabitants until the Day of Calling out.*

It was also said: *dahaha* means "He made it level." Zayd ibn 'Amr said:

*I submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy stones.*
*He spread it out, and when it became level He fastened it with hands, and set upon it the mountains.*

*Al-ṭammah*: the calamity that overwhelms calamities, that is, it rises above them and overcomes them. In their proverbs: "He ran the valley and it overflowed the villages." It is said: "The flood buried the well" when it covered it. *Al-ṭamm* means burial and elevation.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾.

(p. 419) This surah is Meccan. Since the previous surah mentioned the warning of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, this surah swears an oath concerning the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. Since the things sworn by are omitted and their attributes are placed in their stead, and since these attributes have various connections, the scholars differed regarding their intended meaning. 'Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-nazi'at* refers to the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. *Gharqan* means "with great force," which is the intensification of the act; or it means "they drown," meaning the souls of the disbelievers, who drown in Hell. This was said by 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kaysan, and al-Akhfash said: they are the stars that pull from horizon to horizon. Al-Suddi and a group said: they pull toward their Lord through death, and *gharqan* means with intense effort in the chest. Al-Suddi also said: souls yearn for their homelands and strive toward their ways, and they have a pull at the time of death. 'Ata' and 'Ikrima said: they are the bows, and their own strings are pulled by the arrows. 'Ata' also said: they are the groups who pull the bows and other things with great force. Mujahid said: the deaths pull out the souls. It was said: *al-nazi'at* refers to wild animals that pull toward pasture; this was related by Yahya ibn Salam. It was also said: it refers to the warhorses that pull at their bridles, with the bridles drawn out because of the length of their necks, because they are purebred. Those are the ones who leave the house of Islam for the house of war. This was stated in *al-Kashshaf*.

*Al-nasitat*: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the angels bring out the souls at death, meaning they release them and carry them off by God's command to wherever they were destined. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Qatada, al-Hasan, and al-Akhfash: they are the stars that travel from horizon to horizon, moving swiftly. Mujahid also said: they are the deaths. 'Ata' said: they are wild cattle and similar animals that move from region to region. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the souls of believers depart eagerly at death. It was said: they are those that are eager to take life.

*Al-sabihat*: 'Ali and Mujahid said: the angels move about in the horizons by God's command, coming and going. Qatada and al-Hasan said: the stars swim in their orbits. Abu Rawq said: the sun, the moon, the night, and the day. 'Ata' and a group said: horses, since a horse is called *sabih*. It was also said: clouds, because they are like swimmers in the air. It was said: fish, the creatures of the sea and what is below them, and this is from the greatness of created beings, showing that God has extended in this world a variety of living creatures, four hundred of which are on land and six hundred in the sea. 'Ata' also said: ships. Mujahid also said: deaths swim within the souls of living beings.

*Al-sabiqat*: Mujahid said: the angels precede the children of Adam with good and righteous deeds, and Abu Rawq said the same. Ibn Mas'ud said: the souls of believers hasten toward the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for meeting God the Exalted. 'Ata' said: horses. It was said: stars. It was said: deaths precede hopes.

*Al-mudabbirat*: Ibn 'Atiyya said: I know of no disagreement that they are the angels, and the meaning is that they are the ones who manage the affairs which God has subjected and directed them to manage, such as the winds, the clouds, and all other created things. End of quote. It was also said: they are the angels entrusted with various matters: Jibril for revelation, Mikha'il for rain, Israfil for blowing the trumpet, and 'Izra'il for taking souls. It was said: their management consists of descending with what is lawful and unlawful. Mu'adh said: they are the seven planets, and attributing the management to them is metaphorical, meaning that changes of circumstances appear when they conjoin, form squares and sextiles, and other such aspects.

Al-Zamakhshari compiled from these views opinions which he chose and arranged primarily under three categories: the angels, the horses, or the stars. He arranged all the attributes under each of the three, saying: God swore by groups of angels who pull the souls from the bodies, and by the groups who draw them out, meaning they bring them forth, as one draws water from a well when he pulls it up; and by the groups who glide in their passage, meaning they hasten and race ahead toward what they have been commanded, and then manage a matter among the affairs of the servants that benefits them in their religion or their worldly life, as was ordained for them. *Gharqan* means with great intensity in the pulling, that is, they pull it from the far parts of the bodies, from the fingertips and nails. Or He swore by the horses of the warriors who pull at their bridles, up to the end of what we have quoted. Then he said: from your saying "a bull is *nashit*" when it leaves one land for another; and by those that glide in their running and race ahead to the goal, then manage the matter of victory and triumph. The attribution of management to them is because they are among its causes. Or He swore by the stars that pull from the east to the west, and the intensity of their pulling is that they traverse the whole sphere until they descend from the farthest west; and those that come out from one sign of the zodiac to another; and those that glide in the sphere among the planets, then race ahead and manage a matter in the science of calculation.

It was said: *al-nazi'at* are the hands of the warriors or their souls, which pull the bows with the arrows drawn to full extent; and *al-nasitat* are those that take life. End of quote. What appears evident is that what is joined by *fa* is part of the description of the thing sworn by before the *fa*, and that what is joined by *wa* is different from what precedes it, as we established in *al-Mursalat*, although it is also possible that what is joined by *wa* is part of the attributes joined one to another. The preferred view regarding the response to the oath is that it is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected," since what follows indicates it. This was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 2):

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: The answer is: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾. The meaning is: what I have recounted of the Day of Resurrection, and the mention of Musa, peace be upon him, and Fir'awn (Pharaoh). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an ugly view, because the speech has become long. It has also been said that the lam with which the oath is introduced is omitted from His words ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, meaning "for a Day such as this," ﴿followed by the following one﴾. The emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) was not attached, because a separation has occurred between the presumed lam and the verb. Abu Hatim's view is that it is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), as if he had said: ﴿then they will be in the waste land﴾, and ﴿by those who pull out﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' (then) is not used to begin a speech. It has also been said that the construction is: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, and (﴿by those who pull out﴾) is also by inversion, but this is nothing. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa?﴾, because it is in the sense of "qad" (indeed) ("indeed there has come to you"), but this is nothing. All of this is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of one who has not mastered Arabic. Omitting the answer is the correct way, and the view that the lam is omitted from ﴿On the Day it quakes﴾ is closer to this.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid said: "They are the two Blasts, that is, the two Blowings. The first causes everything to die, and in the second everything is brought to life." Mujahid also said: "The quaking one (al-wajifa) is the earthquake, and the following one (al-radifa) is the Blast." Ibn Zayd said: "The quaking one is the earth, and the following one is the Hour." The governing element of (يَوْمَ, yawma, "on the day") is an implied "remember" (udhkur), or "you will certainly be raised" (latub'athunna), which is omitted. The Day is extensive, in which the two Blowings occur, and they are raised in some part of that extensive Day. The phrase ﴿followed by﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that it is a resumptive (mustanif) clause.

Wajifa means "agitated," and the palpitation of the heart results from terror and it results from anxious concern. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Indeed the sons of Hajab and their family,
our livers tremble behind them."

(Qulub, "hearts") is the subject (mubtada'). (Wajifa) is an attributive adjective that governs (yawma'idhin, "on that Day"). (Absaruha, "their eyes") means the eyes of the owners of the hearts. (Khashi'a) is the subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of (qulub). Ibn Atiyya said: "(Qulub) is in the nominative as the subject, and this is permitted even though it is indefinite, because it has been specified by His words (yawma'idhin)." End of quote. But bodies are not specified by time-adverbs; rather, it is specified by His words (wajifa).

(Yaqulun, "they say") describes their state in the world, and the meaning is: they are the ones who say. (Al-hafira): Mujahid said: it is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of a passive (maf'ula). It has also been said that it is in the relative form (nisba), meaning "possessing a hole," and what is meant is the graves, that is, "are we truly to be returned alive in our graves?" Zayd ibn Aslam said: "al-hafira is the Fire." It has also been said that it is the plural of hafira in the sense of "footstep," meaning: "alive, walking on our feet and treading the earth with them." Ibn Abbas said: "The second life is the first condition," and merchants say: "the price is at the hafira," meaning at the beginning of the bargaining. The poet said:

"I swore I would not forget you, so know this,
until people return to the hafira."

Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi Abla read: fi al-hafira without an alif (alif), while the majority read it with the alif. It has been said that they have the same meaning. It has also been said that it is the earth that is barren and changed by the bodies of its dead, from the saying: "his teeth decayed (hafirat) when they were eaten away and changed." Umar, Ubayy, Abdullah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan) and Abu Bakr read: nakhira with an alif. Abu Raja, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-Sulami, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i (p. 421) Qatada, Ibn Wathhab, Ayyub, the people of Makkah, Shibl and the rest of the Seven read without an alif.

﴿They say: "That then would be a losing return."﴾ That is: the return to the hafira, if we are returned. ﴿A losing return﴾: that is, they said this because of their denial of the unseen, meaning: if this were true, our return would be a losing one, since it leads to the Fire. Al-Hasan said: "khasira" means "false," that is, it is not sufficient. This statement from them is mockery. It is narrated that one of the leading men of Quraysh said this. ﴿Then it is but a single shout﴾: when ﴿they say: "Are we indeed to be returned?"﴾ was mentioned, their words contained a suggestion of the improbability of the second creation and belittling of its matter. Therefore the statement ("fa-innama," "then it is but") came in consideration of what their improbability indicated, as if it were said: "What you say is not difficult; it is only one Blast, and then they will be raised, alive, upon the surface of the earth."

Ibn Abbas said: al-Sahira is a land of silver which Allah, the Exalted, creates. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is a mountain in al-Sham (Syria) which Allah, the Exalted, will extend on the Day of Resurrection for the gathering of people. Abu al-Aliya and Sufyan said: it is a land near Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ibn Abbas said: it is the land of Makkah. Qatada said: it is Jahannam (Hell), because there is no sleep for those in it. He saw that the pronouns before it refer to the disbelievers, so he explained it as Jahannam. It has also been said: it is the seventh earth, which Allah will bring, to call the creatures to account upon it.

When they denied the resurrection and rebelled, that grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah, the Exalted, related to him the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and the rebellion of Fir'awn against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he claimed lordship; and what became of Musa, that of salvation, and the state of Fir'awn, that of destruction. This was a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a good tiding of the destruction of those who deny him and of his own salvation from their harm.

So Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you﴾, as an alert for him to gather his mind for what is about to be communicated to him. The discussion of the Sacred Valley has preceded, and the disagreement about the readings of (Tuwa) has been mentioned. ﴿Go to Fir'awn﴾ is an explanation of the call, or it is by implying a verb of saying. ﴿Then say: "Is there in you a desire to purify yourself?"﴾ is gentleness in the invitation, because every sensible person answers such a question with "yes." (Tazakka) means: to adorn oneself with virtues and purify oneself from vices. The purification here includes Islam and the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted. The two men of Madinah (al-Haramiyyan) and Abu Amr, with a variant, read: tazzakka and tassadda, with doubling of the za' and the sad; the rest of the Seven read them with single letters. The Arabs say: "Is there in you a desire (hal laka fi kadha) for such-and-such, or a way (hal ila kadha) to such-and-such?" They omit the condition to which "ila" (to) is attached; meaning: "Do you have a desire or a need for such-and-such, or a path to such-and-such?" The poet said:

"So is there for you in it, for me, since I am
one who sees what baffled the physician Hidhma."

﴿And I guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear﴾: this is an explanation of purification, which is guidance to the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and knowledge of Him. ﴿So that you may fear﴾: that is, fear Him, because fear does not exist except through knowledge. ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. He mentioned fear because it is the essence of the matter. There is an omission in the speech: that is, he went and said to him what his Lord had commanded him, and then followed that with the miracle which indicates his truthfulness. ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾, which was the staff and the hand. He made them one, because the hand is as if it were part of the staff, being subordinate to it; or the staff alone, because it was the foremost and the origin, and the hand was a follower of it, because he used to protect himself with his hand. It has been said that he was told: ﴿Put your hand into your bosom﴾ [al-Naml: 12].

(Fa-kadhdhaba): that is, Fir'awn denied Musa, peace be upon him, and the miracle he brought, and made it a matter of sorcery. (Wa-'asa): that is, he disobeyed Allah, the Exalted, after he knew the truth of what Musa had brought; he only pretended that it was sorcery. ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾. It has been said: "He turned away literally," that is, he rose from his place fleeing by himself. Al-Jumhur said: it is a metaphor for his turning away from faith. (Yas'a): he strove in plotting against Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿Then he gathered﴾: that is, he gathered the magicians and the leaders of his state. (Fa-nada): that is, he stood among them as an orator, or he called out in the place where they had gathered with him. ﴿Then he said: "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ Ibn Atiyya said: "Fir'awn's saying this is the extreme of audacious falsehood, and its like remains among the kings of Egypt and their followers." End of quote.

He only said this because the king of Egypt in his time was an Isma'ili, a doctrine in which they believe in the divinity of their kings. The first of them to rule it was al-Mu'izz ibn al-Mansur ibn al-Qa'im ibn al-Mahdi Ubayd Allah. Al-'Adid governed them, and Allah purified Egypt from this accursed doctrine through the emergence of al-Malik al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub ibn Shadhi, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him on behalf of Islam with good.

﴿So Allah seized him, as a punishment in the Hereafter and in this world﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "The Hereafter" is his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and "the first" is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. It has also been said the reverse. Between his two sayings was a period of forty years. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the punishment of the Hereafter was by burning, and the first, meaning the world, was by drowning. Mujahid said: it is the punishment of the last and first part of his life. Abu Razin said: the first is his disbelief and disobedience, and the last is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. Mujahid also said: it is an expression for the first and last of his sins, meaning: He made an example of all of them.

(Nakala, "punishment") is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), and its governing element is ﴿seized﴾, because it has the same sense. According to al-Mubarrad, it is by implying a verb from its own root, meaning: "He made an example, an example." (Al-nakal) has the sense of (al-tankil, "making an example"), like (al-salam) has the sense of (al-taslim, "greeting"). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿nakala al-akhira﴾ is an emphatic infinitive, like ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 95] and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], as if it were said: "Allah made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first." End of quote. An emphatic infinitive for the content of the preceding clause has an implied governing element from the meaning of the clause.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, in what happened to Fir'awn and the seizure he received, ﴿is a lesson﴾, an admonition, ﴿for whoever fears﴾: that is, for whoever fears the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection and in this world.

**Surat al-Nazi'at is Meccan and has forty-six verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾ ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is it the sky He built?﴾ ﴿He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ ﴿He darkened its night and brought forth its morning light.﴾ ﴿And after that He spread out the earth.﴾ ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture,﴾ ﴿and set the mountains firmly,﴾ ﴿as provision for you and your livestock.﴾ ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes,﴾ ﴿on the Day when man will remember what he strove for,﴾ ﴿and Hellfire will be brought forth for whoever sees,﴾ ﴿then as for whoever transgressed,﴾ ﴿and preferred the worldly life,﴾ ﴿indeed Hellfire will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿But as for whoever feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire,﴾ ﴿indeed Paradise will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained but an evening or a morning.﴾

(p. 417) *Aghraqa fi al-shay'*: he went to the utmost extent in it and reached its end. *Aghraqa al-nazi'* *fi al-qaws*: the archer pulled the bowstring to its full extent until it reached the arrow-head. *Al-istighraq* means comprehensive inclusion, and *al-gharqa* is the shell of an egg. *Nashata al-ba'ir wa al-insan*: he tied the camel or the man. *Anshatahu*: he released him. From this comes the phrase "as if he had been released from a tether." *Nashita*: he went from one region to another. For this reason wild cattle are called *al-nawashit*, because they travel swiftly from place to place. From this is the verse of the poet, who is Himyan ibn Qahafa:

*I see my worries driving the places before me; at times they carry me to Syria, at times to Wasit.*

It seems this word is derived from *al-nashat* (activity). Abu Zayd said: *nashastu al-habl anshuṭuhu nashṭan*: I tied it into a slipknot (*unshuṭa*). *Anshaṭtu*: I untied it. *Anshaṭtu al-habl*: I stretched it. Al-Layth said: *anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭa*: I fastened it, meaning I secured it. *Anshaṭtu al-'iqal*: I stretched its slipknot so that it came undone. It is said that *nashita* has the same meaning as *anshaṭa*. The *unshuṭa* is a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a waistband.

*Wajafa al-qalb wa jiyafan*: the heart pounded from the intensity of fear. Likewise *wajaba wa jiyaban*. In the book *Lughat al-Qur'an* (The Languages of the Qur'an), attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, *wajifa* means "fearful," in the dialect of Hamdan. *Al-hafira*: it is said, "So-and-so returned along his *hafira*," meaning on the path by which he came, since his footsteps have left marks (*hafr*) on it. The Arabs apply the term to the first state to which one returns from its end. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Would you return to the first state with baldness and grey hair? God forbid such folly and shame!*

That is, "Shall I return to youth after baldness and gray hair?"

*Al-nakhira*: that which produces sound through the wind, hollow. *Al-nakhira* has the same meaning, like *ṭami'* and *ṭamia*, *ḥadhir* and *ḥadhar*. This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and a group. It was also said: *al-nakhira* is what is decayed, rotten, and turned into dust. *Nakhira al-'ud wa al-'aẓm*: it decayed and crumbled, and its meaning differs from *al-nakhira*. This is the view of most scholars. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: *al-nakhira* is what has not yet become hollow, and *al-nakhira* is what has already decayed. A rajaz poet said to his horse:

*Advance, brother of the fierce, toward the trials,*
*and let not the heads of the rebels frighten you.*
*Your end is only the dust of the desert,*
*until you return after that to the pit,*
*after you have become hollow bones.*

Another poet said:

*I emptied it of its marrow, so it became like glass vessels in whose hollows the wind whistles.*

It is also narrated as "whistles" (*tuṣaffiru*). *Nukhrat al-rih* (with a *ḍamma* on the *nun*) means the violence of its blowing. *Al-nukhra* also means the front of the nose of a horse, donkey, or pig. One says: "He broke its nukhra." *Al-sahira*: the surface of the earth and the open wilderness. It is described by what happens in it, which is wakefulness (*al-sahar*) due to fear. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*In it is the flesh of the wilderness and the sea, and what they have said remains for them.*

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said:

*They walk in the wilderness, as though its tresses and its locks were the dark garments of a black night.*

*Al-sahur* is like a sheath for the moon, which enters it when it is eclipsed. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said: (p. 418)

*He spread creation upon it when He spread it out, and they are its inhabitants until the Day of Calling out.*

It was also said: *dahaha* means "He made it level." Zayd ibn 'Amr said:

*I submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy stones.*
*He spread it out, and when it became level He fastened it with hands, and set upon it the mountains.*

*Al-ṭammah*: the calamity that overwhelms calamities, that is, it rises above them and overcomes them. In their proverbs: "He ran the valley and it overflowed the villages." It is said: "The flood buried the well" when it covered it. *Al-ṭamm* means burial and elevation.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾.

(p. 419) This surah is Meccan. Since the previous surah mentioned the warning of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, this surah swears an oath concerning the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. Since the things sworn by are omitted and their attributes are placed in their stead, and since these attributes have various connections, the scholars differed regarding their intended meaning. 'Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-nazi'at* refers to the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. *Gharqan* means "with great force," which is the intensification of the act; or it means "they drown," meaning the souls of the disbelievers, who drown in Hell. This was said by 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kaysan, and al-Akhfash said: they are the stars that pull from horizon to horizon. Al-Suddi and a group said: they pull toward their Lord through death, and *gharqan* means with intense effort in the chest. Al-Suddi also said: souls yearn for their homelands and strive toward their ways, and they have a pull at the time of death. 'Ata' and 'Ikrima said: they are the bows, and their own strings are pulled by the arrows. 'Ata' also said: they are the groups who pull the bows and other things with great force. Mujahid said: the deaths pull out the souls. It was said: *al-nazi'at* refers to wild animals that pull toward pasture; this was related by Yahya ibn Salam. It was also said: it refers to the warhorses that pull at their bridles, with the bridles drawn out because of the length of their necks, because they are purebred. Those are the ones who leave the house of Islam for the house of war. This was stated in *al-Kashshaf*.

*Al-nasitat*: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the angels bring out the souls at death, meaning they release them and carry them off by God's command to wherever they were destined. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Qatada, al-Hasan, and al-Akhfash: they are the stars that travel from horizon to horizon, moving swiftly. Mujahid also said: they are the deaths. 'Ata' said: they are wild cattle and similar animals that move from region to region. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the souls of believers depart eagerly at death. It was said: they are those that are eager to take life.

*Al-sabihat*: 'Ali and Mujahid said: the angels move about in the horizons by God's command, coming and going. Qatada and al-Hasan said: the stars swim in their orbits. Abu Rawq said: the sun, the moon, the night, and the day. 'Ata' and a group said: horses, since a horse is called *sabih*. It was also said: clouds, because they are like swimmers in the air. It was said: fish, the creatures of the sea and what is below them, and this is from the greatness of created beings, showing that God has extended in this world a variety of living creatures, four hundred of which are on land and six hundred in the sea. 'Ata' also said: ships. Mujahid also said: deaths swim within the souls of living beings.

*Al-sabiqat*: Mujahid said: the angels precede the children of Adam with good and righteous deeds, and Abu Rawq said the same. Ibn Mas'ud said: the souls of believers hasten toward the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for meeting God the Exalted. 'Ata' said: horses. It was said: stars. It was said: deaths precede hopes.

*Al-mudabbirat*: Ibn 'Atiyya said: I know of no disagreement that they are the angels, and the meaning is that they are the ones who manage the affairs which God has subjected and directed them to manage, such as the winds, the clouds, and all other created things. End of quote. It was also said: they are the angels entrusted with various matters: Jibril for revelation, Mikha'il for rain, Israfil for blowing the trumpet, and 'Izra'il for taking souls. It was said: their management consists of descending with what is lawful and unlawful. Mu'adh said: they are the seven planets, and attributing the management to them is metaphorical, meaning that changes of circumstances appear when they conjoin, form squares and sextiles, and other such aspects.

Al-Zamakhshari compiled from these views opinions which he chose and arranged primarily under three categories: the angels, the horses, or the stars. He arranged all the attributes under each of the three, saying: God swore by groups of angels who pull the souls from the bodies, and by the groups who draw them out, meaning they bring them forth, as one draws water from a well when he pulls it up; and by the groups who glide in their passage, meaning they hasten and race ahead toward what they have been commanded, and then manage a matter among the affairs of the servants that benefits them in their religion or their worldly life, as was ordained for them. *Gharqan* means with great intensity in the pulling, that is, they pull it from the far parts of the bodies, from the fingertips and nails. Or He swore by the horses of the warriors who pull at their bridles, up to the end of what we have quoted. Then he said: from your saying "a bull is *nashit*" when it leaves one land for another; and by those that glide in their running and race ahead to the goal, then manage the matter of victory and triumph. The attribution of management to them is because they are among its causes. Or He swore by the stars that pull from the east to the west, and the intensity of their pulling is that they traverse the whole sphere until they descend from the farthest west; and those that come out from one sign of the zodiac to another; and those that glide in the sphere among the planets, then race ahead and manage a matter in the science of calculation.

It was said: *al-nazi'at* are the hands of the warriors or their souls, which pull the bows with the arrows drawn to full extent; and *al-nasitat* are those that take life. End of quote. What appears evident is that what is joined by *fa* is part of the description of the thing sworn by before the *fa*, and that what is joined by *wa* is different from what precedes it, as we established in *al-Mursalat*, although it is also possible that what is joined by *wa* is part of the attributes joined one to another. The preferred view regarding the response to the oath is that it is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected," since what follows indicates it. This was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 2):

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: The answer is: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾. The meaning is: what I have recounted of the Day of Resurrection, and the mention of Musa, peace be upon him, and Fir'awn (Pharaoh). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an ugly view, because the speech has become long. It has also been said that the lam with which the oath is introduced is omitted from His words ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, meaning "for a Day such as this," ﴿followed by the following one﴾. The emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) was not attached, because a separation has occurred between the presumed lam and the verb. Abu Hatim's view is that it is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), as if he had said: ﴿then they will be in the waste land﴾, and ﴿by those who pull out﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' (then) is not used to begin a speech. It has also been said that the construction is: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, and (﴿by those who pull out﴾) is also by inversion, but this is nothing. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa?﴾, because it is in the sense of "qad" (indeed) ("indeed there has come to you"), but this is nothing. All of this is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of one who has not mastered Arabic. Omitting the answer is the correct way, and the view that the lam is omitted from ﴿On the Day it quakes﴾ is closer to this.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid said: "They are the two Blasts, that is, the two Blowings. The first causes everything to die, and in the second everything is brought to life." Mujahid also said: "The quaking one (al-wajifa) is the earthquake, and the following one (al-radifa) is the Blast." Ibn Zayd said: "The quaking one is the earth, and the following one is the Hour." The governing element of (يَوْمَ, yawma, "on the day") is an implied "remember" (udhkur), or "you will certainly be raised" (latub'athunna), which is omitted. The Day is extensive, in which the two Blowings occur, and they are raised in some part of that extensive Day. The phrase ﴿followed by﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that it is a resumptive (mustanif) clause.

Wajifa means "agitated," and the palpitation of the heart results from terror and it results from anxious concern. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Indeed the sons of Hajab and their family,
our livers tremble behind them."

(Qulub, "hearts") is the subject (mubtada'). (Wajifa) is an attributive adjective that governs (yawma'idhin, "on that Day"). (Absaruha, "their eyes") means the eyes of the owners of the hearts. (Khashi'a) is the subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of (qulub). Ibn Atiyya said: "(Qulub) is in the nominative as the subject, and this is permitted even though it is indefinite, because it has been specified by His words (yawma'idhin)." End of quote. But bodies are not specified by time-adverbs; rather, it is specified by His words (wajifa).

(Yaqulun, "they say") describes their state in the world, and the meaning is: they are the ones who say. (Al-hafira): Mujahid said: it is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of a passive (maf'ula). It has also been said that it is in the relative form (nisba), meaning "possessing a hole," and what is meant is the graves, that is, "are we truly to be returned alive in our graves?" Zayd ibn Aslam said: "al-hafira is the Fire." It has also been said that it is the plural of hafira in the sense of "footstep," meaning: "alive, walking on our feet and treading the earth with them." Ibn Abbas said: "The second life is the first condition," and merchants say: "the price is at the hafira," meaning at the beginning of the bargaining. The poet said:

"I swore I would not forget you, so know this,
until people return to the hafira."

Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi Abla read: fi al-hafira without an alif (alif), while the majority read it with the alif. It has been said that they have the same meaning. It has also been said that it is the earth that is barren and changed by the bodies of its dead, from the saying: "his teeth decayed (hafirat) when they were eaten away and changed." Umar, Ubayy, Abdullah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan) and Abu Bakr read: nakhira with an alif. Abu Raja, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-Sulami, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i (p. 421) Qatada, Ibn Wathhab, Ayyub, the people of Makkah, Shibl and the rest of the Seven read without an alif.

﴿They say: "That then would be a losing return."﴾ That is: the return to the hafira, if we are returned. ﴿A losing return﴾: that is, they said this because of their denial of the unseen, meaning: if this were true, our return would be a losing one, since it leads to the Fire. Al-Hasan said: "khasira" means "false," that is, it is not sufficient. This statement from them is mockery. It is narrated that one of the leading men of Quraysh said this. ﴿Then it is but a single shout﴾: when ﴿they say: "Are we indeed to be returned?"﴾ was mentioned, their words contained a suggestion of the improbability of the second creation and belittling of its matter. Therefore the statement ("fa-innama," "then it is but") came in consideration of what their improbability indicated, as if it were said: "What you say is not difficult; it is only one Blast, and then they will be raised, alive, upon the surface of the earth."

Ibn Abbas said: al-Sahira is a land of silver which Allah, the Exalted, creates. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is a mountain in al-Sham (Syria) which Allah, the Exalted, will extend on the Day of Resurrection for the gathering of people. Abu al-Aliya and Sufyan said: it is a land near Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ibn Abbas said: it is the land of Makkah. Qatada said: it is Jahannam (Hell), because there is no sleep for those in it. He saw that the pronouns before it refer to the disbelievers, so he explained it as Jahannam. It has also been said: it is the seventh earth, which Allah will bring, to call the creatures to account upon it.

When they denied the resurrection and rebelled, that grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah, the Exalted, related to him the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and the rebellion of Fir'awn against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he claimed lordship; and what became of Musa, that of salvation, and the state of Fir'awn, that of destruction. This was a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a good tiding of the destruction of those who deny him and of his own salvation from their harm.

So Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you﴾, as an alert for him to gather his mind for what is about to be communicated to him. The discussion of the Sacred Valley has preceded, and the disagreement about the readings of (Tuwa) has been mentioned. ﴿Go to Fir'awn﴾ is an explanation of the call, or it is by implying a verb of saying. ﴿Then say: "Is there in you a desire to purify yourself?"﴾ is gentleness in the invitation, because every sensible person answers such a question with "yes." (Tazakka) means: to adorn oneself with virtues and purify oneself from vices. The purification here includes Islam and the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted. The two men of Madinah (al-Haramiyyan) and Abu Amr, with a variant, read: tazzakka and tassadda, with doubling of the za' and the sad; the rest of the Seven read them with single letters. The Arabs say: "Is there in you a desire (hal laka fi kadha) for such-and-such, or a way (hal ila kadha) to such-and-such?" They omit the condition to which "ila" (to) is attached; meaning: "Do you have a desire or a need for such-and-such, or a path to such-and-such?" The poet said:

"So is there for you in it, for me, since I am
one who sees what baffled the physician Hidhma."

﴿And I guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear﴾: this is an explanation of purification, which is guidance to the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and knowledge of Him. ﴿So that you may fear﴾: that is, fear Him, because fear does not exist except through knowledge. ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. He mentioned fear because it is the essence of the matter. There is an omission in the speech: that is, he went and said to him what his Lord had commanded him, and then followed that with the miracle which indicates his truthfulness. ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾, which was the staff and the hand. He made them one, because the hand is as if it were part of the staff, being subordinate to it; or the staff alone, because it was the foremost and the origin, and the hand was a follower of it, because he used to protect himself with his hand. It has been said that he was told: ﴿Put your hand into your bosom﴾ [al-Naml: 12].

(Fa-kadhdhaba): that is, Fir'awn denied Musa, peace be upon him, and the miracle he brought, and made it a matter of sorcery. (Wa-'asa): that is, he disobeyed Allah, the Exalted, after he knew the truth of what Musa had brought; he only pretended that it was sorcery. ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾. It has been said: "He turned away literally," that is, he rose from his place fleeing by himself. Al-Jumhur said: it is a metaphor for his turning away from faith. (Yas'a): he strove in plotting against Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿Then he gathered﴾: that is, he gathered the magicians and the leaders of his state. (Fa-nada): that is, he stood among them as an orator, or he called out in the place where they had gathered with him. ﴿Then he said: "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ Ibn Atiyya said: "Fir'awn's saying this is the extreme of audacious falsehood, and its like remains among the kings of Egypt and their followers." End of quote.

He only said this because the king of Egypt in his time was an Isma'ili, a doctrine in which they believe in the divinity of their kings. The first of them to rule it was al-Mu'izz ibn al-Mansur ibn al-Qa'im ibn al-Mahdi Ubayd Allah. Al-'Adid governed them, and Allah purified Egypt from this accursed doctrine through the emergence of al-Malik al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub ibn Shadhi, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him on behalf of Islam with good.

﴿So Allah seized him, as a punishment in the Hereafter and in this world﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "The Hereafter" is his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and "the first" is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. It has also been said the reverse. Between his two sayings was a period of forty years. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the punishment of the Hereafter was by burning, and the first, meaning the world, was by drowning. Mujahid said: it is the punishment of the last and first part of his life. Abu Razin said: the first is his disbelief and disobedience, and the last is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. Mujahid also said: it is an expression for the first and last of his sins, meaning: He made an example of all of them.

(Nakala, "punishment") is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), and its governing element is ﴿seized﴾, because it has the same sense. According to al-Mubarrad, it is by implying a verb from its own root, meaning: "He made an example, an example." (Al-nakal) has the sense of (al-tankil, "making an example"), like (al-salam) has the sense of (al-taslim, "greeting"). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿nakala al-akhira﴾ is an emphatic infinitive, like ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 95] and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], as if it were said: "Allah made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first." End of quote. An emphatic infinitive for the content of the preceding clause has an implied governing element from the meaning of the clause.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, in what happened to Fir'awn and the seizure he received, ﴿is a lesson﴾, an admonition, ﴿for whoever fears﴾: that is, for whoever fears the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection and in this world.

**Surat al-Nazi'at is Meccan and has forty-six verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾ ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is it the sky He built?﴾ ﴿He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ ﴿He darkened its night and brought forth its morning light.﴾ ﴿And after that He spread out the earth.﴾ ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture,﴾ ﴿and set the mountains firmly,﴾ ﴿as provision for you and your livestock.﴾ ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes,﴾ ﴿on the Day when man will remember what he strove for,﴾ ﴿and Hellfire will be brought forth for whoever sees,﴾ ﴿then as for whoever transgressed,﴾ ﴿and preferred the worldly life,﴾ ﴿indeed Hellfire will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿But as for whoever feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire,﴾ ﴿indeed Paradise will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained but an evening or a morning.﴾

(p. 417) *Aghraqa fi al-shay'*: he went to the utmost extent in it and reached its end. *Aghraqa al-nazi'* *fi al-qaws*: the archer pulled the bowstring to its full extent until it reached the arrow-head. *Al-istighraq* means comprehensive inclusion, and *al-gharqa* is the shell of an egg. *Nashata al-ba'ir wa al-insan*: he tied the camel or the man. *Anshatahu*: he released him. From this comes the phrase "as if he had been released from a tether." *Nashita*: he went from one region to another. For this reason wild cattle are called *al-nawashit*, because they travel swiftly from place to place. From this is the verse of the poet, who is Himyan ibn Qahafa:

*I see my worries driving the places before me; at times they carry me to Syria, at times to Wasit.*

It seems this word is derived from *al-nashat* (activity). Abu Zayd said: *nashastu al-habl anshuṭuhu nashṭan*: I tied it into a slipknot (*unshuṭa*). *Anshaṭtu*: I untied it. *Anshaṭtu al-habl*: I stretched it. Al-Layth said: *anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭa*: I fastened it, meaning I secured it. *Anshaṭtu al-'iqal*: I stretched its slipknot so that it came undone. It is said that *nashita* has the same meaning as *anshaṭa*. The *unshuṭa* is a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a waistband.

*Wajafa al-qalb wa jiyafan*: the heart pounded from the intensity of fear. Likewise *wajaba wa jiyaban*. In the book *Lughat al-Qur'an* (The Languages of the Qur'an), attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, *wajifa* means "fearful," in the dialect of Hamdan. *Al-hafira*: it is said, "So-and-so returned along his *hafira*," meaning on the path by which he came, since his footsteps have left marks (*hafr*) on it. The Arabs apply the term to the first state to which one returns from its end. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Would you return to the first state with baldness and grey hair? God forbid such folly and shame!*

That is, "Shall I return to youth after baldness and gray hair?"

*Al-nakhira*: that which produces sound through the wind, hollow. *Al-nakhira* has the same meaning, like *ṭami'* and *ṭamia*, *ḥadhir* and *ḥadhar*. This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and a group. It was also said: *al-nakhira* is what is decayed, rotten, and turned into dust. *Nakhira al-'ud wa al-'aẓm*: it decayed and crumbled, and its meaning differs from *al-nakhira*. This is the view of most scholars. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: *al-nakhira* is what has not yet become hollow, and *al-nakhira* is what has already decayed. A rajaz poet said to his horse:

*Advance, brother of the fierce, toward the trials,*
*and let not the heads of the rebels frighten you.*
*Your end is only the dust of the desert,*
*until you return after that to the pit,*
*after you have become hollow bones.*

Another poet said:

*I emptied it of its marrow, so it became like glass vessels in whose hollows the wind whistles.*

It is also narrated as "whistles" (*tuṣaffiru*). *Nukhrat al-rih* (with a *ḍamma* on the *nun*) means the violence of its blowing. *Al-nukhra* also means the front of the nose of a horse, donkey, or pig. One says: "He broke its nukhra." *Al-sahira*: the surface of the earth and the open wilderness. It is described by what happens in it, which is wakefulness (*al-sahar*) due to fear. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*In it is the flesh of the wilderness and the sea, and what they have said remains for them.*

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said:

*They walk in the wilderness, as though its tresses and its locks were the dark garments of a black night.*

*Al-sahur* is like a sheath for the moon, which enters it when it is eclipsed. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said: (p. 418)

*He spread creation upon it when He spread it out, and they are its inhabitants until the Day of Calling out.*

It was also said: *dahaha* means "He made it level." Zayd ibn 'Amr said:

*I submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy stones.*
*He spread it out, and when it became level He fastened it with hands, and set upon it the mountains.*

*Al-ṭammah*: the calamity that overwhelms calamities, that is, it rises above them and overcomes them. In their proverbs: "He ran the valley and it overflowed the villages." It is said: "The flood buried the well" when it covered it. *Al-ṭamm* means burial and elevation.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾.

(p. 419) This surah is Meccan. Since the previous surah mentioned the warning of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, this surah swears an oath concerning the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. Since the things sworn by are omitted and their attributes are placed in their stead, and since these attributes have various connections, the scholars differed regarding their intended meaning. 'Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-nazi'at* refers to the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. *Gharqan* means "with great force," which is the intensification of the act; or it means "they drown," meaning the souls of the disbelievers, who drown in Hell. This was said by 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kaysan, and al-Akhfash said: they are the stars that pull from horizon to horizon. Al-Suddi and a group said: they pull toward their Lord through death, and *gharqan* means with intense effort in the chest. Al-Suddi also said: souls yearn for their homelands and strive toward their ways, and they have a pull at the time of death. 'Ata' and 'Ikrima said: they are the bows, and their own strings are pulled by the arrows. 'Ata' also said: they are the groups who pull the bows and other things with great force. Mujahid said: the deaths pull out the souls. It was said: *al-nazi'at* refers to wild animals that pull toward pasture; this was related by Yahya ibn Salam. It was also said: it refers to the warhorses that pull at their bridles, with the bridles drawn out because of the length of their necks, because they are purebred. Those are the ones who leave the house of Islam for the house of war. This was stated in *al-Kashshaf*.

*Al-nasitat*: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the angels bring out the souls at death, meaning they release them and carry them off by God's command to wherever they were destined. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Qatada, al-Hasan, and al-Akhfash: they are the stars that travel from horizon to horizon, moving swiftly. Mujahid also said: they are the deaths. 'Ata' said: they are wild cattle and similar animals that move from region to region. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the souls of believers depart eagerly at death. It was said: they are those that are eager to take life.

*Al-sabihat*: 'Ali and Mujahid said: the angels move about in the horizons by God's command, coming and going. Qatada and al-Hasan said: the stars swim in their orbits. Abu Rawq said: the sun, the moon, the night, and the day. 'Ata' and a group said: horses, since a horse is called *sabih*. It was also said: clouds, because they are like swimmers in the air. It was said: fish, the creatures of the sea and what is below them, and this is from the greatness of created beings, showing that God has extended in this world a variety of living creatures, four hundred of which are on land and six hundred in the sea. 'Ata' also said: ships. Mujahid also said: deaths swim within the souls of living beings.

*Al-sabiqat*: Mujahid said: the angels precede the children of Adam with good and righteous deeds, and Abu Rawq said the same. Ibn Mas'ud said: the souls of believers hasten toward the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for meeting God the Exalted. 'Ata' said: horses. It was said: stars. It was said: deaths precede hopes.

*Al-mudabbirat*: Ibn 'Atiyya said: I know of no disagreement that they are the angels, and the meaning is that they are the ones who manage the affairs which God has subjected and directed them to manage, such as the winds, the clouds, and all other created things. End of quote. It was also said: they are the angels entrusted with various matters: Jibril for revelation, Mikha'il for rain, Israfil for blowing the trumpet, and 'Izra'il for taking souls. It was said: their management consists of descending with what is lawful and unlawful. Mu'adh said: they are the seven planets, and attributing the management to them is metaphorical, meaning that changes of circumstances appear when they conjoin, form squares and sextiles, and other such aspects.

Al-Zamakhshari compiled from these views opinions which he chose and arranged primarily under three categories: the angels, the horses, or the stars. He arranged all the attributes under each of the three, saying: God swore by groups of angels who pull the souls from the bodies, and by the groups who draw them out, meaning they bring them forth, as one draws water from a well when he pulls it up; and by the groups who glide in their passage, meaning they hasten and race ahead toward what they have been commanded, and then manage a matter among the affairs of the servants that benefits them in their religion or their worldly life, as was ordained for them. *Gharqan* means with great intensity in the pulling, that is, they pull it from the far parts of the bodies, from the fingertips and nails. Or He swore by the horses of the warriors who pull at their bridles, up to the end of what we have quoted. Then he said: from your saying "a bull is *nashit*" when it leaves one land for another; and by those that glide in their running and race ahead to the goal, then manage the matter of victory and triumph. The attribution of management to them is because they are among its causes. Or He swore by the stars that pull from the east to the west, and the intensity of their pulling is that they traverse the whole sphere until they descend from the farthest west; and those that come out from one sign of the zodiac to another; and those that glide in the sphere among the planets, then race ahead and manage a matter in the science of calculation.

It was said: *al-nazi'at* are the hands of the warriors or their souls, which pull the bows with the arrows drawn to full extent; and *al-nasitat* are those that take life. End of quote. What appears evident is that what is joined by *fa* is part of the description of the thing sworn by before the *fa*, and that what is joined by *wa* is different from what precedes it, as we established in *al-Mursalat*, although it is also possible that what is joined by *wa* is part of the attributes joined one to another. The preferred view regarding the response to the oath is that it is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected," since what follows indicates it. This was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 2):

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: The answer is: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾. The meaning is: what I have recounted of the Day of Resurrection, and the mention of Musa, peace be upon him, and Fir'awn (Pharaoh). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an ugly view, because the speech has become long. It has also been said that the lam with which the oath is introduced is omitted from His words ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, meaning "for a Day such as this," ﴿followed by the following one﴾. The emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) was not attached, because a separation has occurred between the presumed lam and the verb. Abu Hatim's view is that it is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), as if he had said: ﴿then they will be in the waste land﴾, and ﴿by those who pull out﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' (then) is not used to begin a speech. It has also been said that the construction is: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, and (﴿by those who pull out﴾) is also by inversion, but this is nothing. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa?﴾, because it is in the sense of "qad" (indeed) ("indeed there has come to you"), but this is nothing. All of this is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of one who has not mastered Arabic. Omitting the answer is the correct way, and the view that the lam is omitted from ﴿On the Day it quakes﴾ is closer to this.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid said: "They are the two Blasts, that is, the two Blowings. The first causes everything to die, and in the second everything is brought to life." Mujahid also said: "The quaking one (al-wajifa) is the earthquake, and the following one (al-radifa) is the Blast." Ibn Zayd said: "The quaking one is the earth, and the following one is the Hour." The governing element of (يَوْمَ, yawma, "on the day") is an implied "remember" (udhkur), or "you will certainly be raised" (latub'athunna), which is omitted. The Day is extensive, in which the two Blowings occur, and they are raised in some part of that extensive Day. The phrase ﴿followed by﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that it is a resumptive (mustanif) clause.

Wajifa means "agitated," and the palpitation of the heart results from terror and it results from anxious concern. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Indeed the sons of Hajab and their family,
our livers tremble behind them."

(Qulub, "hearts") is the subject (mubtada'). (Wajifa) is an attributive adjective that governs (yawma'idhin, "on that Day"). (Absaruha, "their eyes") means the eyes of the owners of the hearts. (Khashi'a) is the subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of (qulub). Ibn Atiyya said: "(Qulub) is in the nominative as the subject, and this is permitted even though it is indefinite, because it has been specified by His words (yawma'idhin)." End of quote. But bodies are not specified by time-adverbs; rather, it is specified by His words (wajifa).

(Yaqulun, "they say") describes their state in the world, and the meaning is: they are the ones who say. (Al-hafira): Mujahid said: it is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of a passive (maf'ula). It has also been said that it is in the relative form (nisba), meaning "possessing a hole," and what is meant is the graves, that is, "are we truly to be returned alive in our graves?" Zayd ibn Aslam said: "al-hafira is the Fire." It has also been said that it is the plural of hafira in the sense of "footstep," meaning: "alive, walking on our feet and treading the earth with them." Ibn Abbas said: "The second life is the first condition," and merchants say: "the price is at the hafira," meaning at the beginning of the bargaining. The poet said:

"I swore I would not forget you, so know this,
until people return to the hafira."

Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi Abla read: fi al-hafira without an alif (alif), while the majority read it with the alif. It has been said that they have the same meaning. It has also been said that it is the earth that is barren and changed by the bodies of its dead, from the saying: "his teeth decayed (hafirat) when they were eaten away and changed." Umar, Ubayy, Abdullah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan) and Abu Bakr read: nakhira with an alif. Abu Raja, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-Sulami, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i (p. 421) Qatada, Ibn Wathhab, Ayyub, the people of Makkah, Shibl and the rest of the Seven read without an alif.

﴿They say: "That then would be a losing return."﴾ That is: the return to the hafira, if we are returned. ﴿A losing return﴾: that is, they said this because of their denial of the unseen, meaning: if this were true, our return would be a losing one, since it leads to the Fire. Al-Hasan said: "khasira" means "false," that is, it is not sufficient. This statement from them is mockery. It is narrated that one of the leading men of Quraysh said this. ﴿Then it is but a single shout﴾: when ﴿they say: "Are we indeed to be returned?"﴾ was mentioned, their words contained a suggestion of the improbability of the second creation and belittling of its matter. Therefore the statement ("fa-innama," "then it is but") came in consideration of what their improbability indicated, as if it were said: "What you say is not difficult; it is only one Blast, and then they will be raised, alive, upon the surface of the earth."

Ibn Abbas said: al-Sahira is a land of silver which Allah, the Exalted, creates. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is a mountain in al-Sham (Syria) which Allah, the Exalted, will extend on the Day of Resurrection for the gathering of people. Abu al-Aliya and Sufyan said: it is a land near Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ibn Abbas said: it is the land of Makkah. Qatada said: it is Jahannam (Hell), because there is no sleep for those in it. He saw that the pronouns before it refer to the disbelievers, so he explained it as Jahannam. It has also been said: it is the seventh earth, which Allah will bring, to call the creatures to account upon it.

When they denied the resurrection and rebelled, that grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah, the Exalted, related to him the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and the rebellion of Fir'awn against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he claimed lordship; and what became of Musa, that of salvation, and the state of Fir'awn, that of destruction. This was a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a good tiding of the destruction of those who deny him and of his own salvation from their harm.

So Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you﴾, as an alert for him to gather his mind for what is about to be communicated to him. The discussion of the Sacred Valley has preceded, and the disagreement about the readings of (Tuwa) has been mentioned. ﴿Go to Fir'awn﴾ is an explanation of the call, or it is by implying a verb of saying. ﴿Then say: "Is there in you a desire to purify yourself?"﴾ is gentleness in the invitation, because every sensible person answers such a question with "yes." (Tazakka) means: to adorn oneself with virtues and purify oneself from vices. The purification here includes Islam and the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted. The two men of Madinah (al-Haramiyyan) and Abu Amr, with a variant, read: tazzakka and tassadda, with doubling of the za' and the sad; the rest of the Seven read them with single letters. The Arabs say: "Is there in you a desire (hal laka fi kadha) for such-and-such, or a way (hal ila kadha) to such-and-such?" They omit the condition to which "ila" (to) is attached; meaning: "Do you have a desire or a need for such-and-such, or a path to such-and-such?" The poet said:

"So is there for you in it, for me, since I am
one who sees what baffled the physician Hidhma."

﴿And I guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear﴾: this is an explanation of purification, which is guidance to the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and knowledge of Him. ﴿So that you may fear﴾: that is, fear Him, because fear does not exist except through knowledge. ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. He mentioned fear because it is the essence of the matter. There is an omission in the speech: that is, he went and said to him what his Lord had commanded him, and then followed that with the miracle which indicates his truthfulness. ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾, which was the staff and the hand. He made them one, because the hand is as if it were part of the staff, being subordinate to it; or the staff alone, because it was the foremost and the origin, and the hand was a follower of it, because he used to protect himself with his hand. It has been said that he was told: ﴿Put your hand into your bosom﴾ [al-Naml: 12].

(Fa-kadhdhaba): that is, Fir'awn denied Musa, peace be upon him, and the miracle he brought, and made it a matter of sorcery. (Wa-'asa): that is, he disobeyed Allah, the Exalted, after he knew the truth of what Musa had brought; he only pretended that it was sorcery. ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾. It has been said: "He turned away literally," that is, he rose from his place fleeing by himself. Al-Jumhur said: it is a metaphor for his turning away from faith. (Yas'a): he strove in plotting against Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿Then he gathered﴾: that is, he gathered the magicians and the leaders of his state. (Fa-nada): that is, he stood among them as an orator, or he called out in the place where they had gathered with him. ﴿Then he said: "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ Ibn Atiyya said: "Fir'awn's saying this is the extreme of audacious falsehood, and its like remains among the kings of Egypt and their followers." End of quote.

He only said this because the king of Egypt in his time was an Isma'ili, a doctrine in which they believe in the divinity of their kings. The first of them to rule it was al-Mu'izz ibn al-Mansur ibn al-Qa'im ibn al-Mahdi Ubayd Allah. Al-'Adid governed them, and Allah purified Egypt from this accursed doctrine through the emergence of al-Malik al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub ibn Shadhi, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him on behalf of Islam with good.

﴿So Allah seized him, as a punishment in the Hereafter and in this world﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "The Hereafter" is his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and "the first" is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. It has also been said the reverse. Between his two sayings was a period of forty years. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the punishment of the Hereafter was by burning, and the first, meaning the world, was by drowning. Mujahid said: it is the punishment of the last and first part of his life. Abu Razin said: the first is his disbelief and disobedience, and the last is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. Mujahid also said: it is an expression for the first and last of his sins, meaning: He made an example of all of them.

(Nakala, "punishment") is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), and its governing element is ﴿seized﴾, because it has the same sense. According to al-Mubarrad, it is by implying a verb from its own root, meaning: "He made an example, an example." (Al-nakal) has the sense of (al-tankil, "making an example"), like (al-salam) has the sense of (al-taslim, "greeting"). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿nakala al-akhira﴾ is an emphatic infinitive, like ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 95] and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], as if it were said: "Allah made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first." End of quote. An emphatic infinitive for the content of the preceding clause has an implied governing element from the meaning of the clause.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, in what happened to Fir'awn and the seizure he received, ﴿is a lesson﴾, an admonition, ﴿for whoever fears﴾: that is, for whoever fears the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection and in this world.

**Surat al-Nazi'at is Meccan and has forty-six verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By those who pull out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿then those who manage affairs,﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Quaking shakes,﴾ ﴿followed by the Following.﴾ ﴿Hearts that Day will be pounding,﴾ ﴿their eyes downcast.﴾ ﴿They say: "Shall we really be returned to our former state?﴾ ﴿Even when we have become crumbling bones?"﴾ ﴿They say: "That would then be a losing return."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast,﴾ ﴿and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa,﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Say: Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him."﴾ ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign,﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away, striving.﴾ ﴿He gathered and called out,﴾ ﴿saying, "I am your Lord, the Most High."﴾ ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾ ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is it the sky He built?﴾ ﴿He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ ﴿He darkened its night and brought forth its morning light.﴾ ﴿And after that He spread out the earth.﴾ ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture,﴾ ﴿and set the mountains firmly,﴾ ﴿as provision for you and your livestock.﴾ ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes,﴾ ﴿on the Day when man will remember what he strove for,﴾ ﴿and Hellfire will be brought forth for whoever sees,﴾ ﴿then as for whoever transgressed,﴾ ﴿and preferred the worldly life,﴾ ﴿indeed Hellfire will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿But as for whoever feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire,﴾ ﴿indeed Paradise will be his refuge.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained but an evening or a morning.﴾

(p. 417) *Aghraqa fi al-shay'*: he went to the utmost extent in it and reached its end. *Aghraqa al-nazi'* *fi al-qaws*: the archer pulled the bowstring to its full extent until it reached the arrow-head. *Al-istighraq* means comprehensive inclusion, and *al-gharqa* is the shell of an egg. *Nashata al-ba'ir wa al-insan*: he tied the camel or the man. *Anshatahu*: he released him. From this comes the phrase "as if he had been released from a tether." *Nashita*: he went from one region to another. For this reason wild cattle are called *al-nawashit*, because they travel swiftly from place to place. From this is the verse of the poet, who is Himyan ibn Qahafa:

*I see my worries driving the places before me; at times they carry me to Syria, at times to Wasit.*

It seems this word is derived from *al-nashat* (activity). Abu Zayd said: *nashastu al-habl anshuṭuhu nashṭan*: I tied it into a slipknot (*unshuṭa*). *Anshaṭtu*: I untied it. *Anshaṭtu al-habl*: I stretched it. Al-Layth said: *anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭa*: I fastened it, meaning I secured it. *Anshaṭtu al-'iqal*: I stretched its slipknot so that it came undone.
